title: Ravana and Maricha's warning
hook: flatterers are everywhere, says an old rakshasa to his king; the person who tells you the hard truth is rare
carry: pleasant things are easy to find
tomorrow: Ravana and Maricha's warning, part three

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ravana and Maricha's warning, part one. Maricha talked Ravana out of the plan, until Shurpanakha shamed him in his court: pride stung in public is harder to talk down. Did you wait before deciding with stung pride? Day five hundred sixty-six.

Ravana sets out again in his flying chariot, along the coast. Valmiki slows down to paint it: the shore lined with coconut palms and sandalwood, pearls drying on the beaches, hermitages of sages, and the ships of merchants. Then the chariot lands at Maricha's hermitage for the second time. The old rakshasa, in bark clothes and matted hair, welcomes his king with food and water, and then asks, carefully: why have you come back?
screen: `A FLYING CHARIOT ALONG THE COAST.` → `PEARLS ON THE BEACHES.` → `WHY HAVE YOU COME BACK?`

segments.voice: Ravana spells out the plan. Turn yourself into a golden deer, spotted with silver, and wander near Rama's hut. Sita will want you. Rama and Lakshmana will go after you. Then I'll take her. Maricha begins with a saying: people who say pleasant things are always easy to find, king. But someone who says what is unpleasant and good for you, and someone who will listen to it, those are rare. Then he tells Ravana the truth he doesn't want. You don't know who Rama is. He wasn't sent to the forest for any crime. He went to keep his father's word. And then a short line in Sanskrit, ramo vigrahavan dharmah: Rama is dharma in bodily form. Right living, duty, truth, with a body and a bow. To steal his wife, Maricha says, is to walk into a fire. You'll ruin yourself, your city and your people. Notice who's speaking. Not a sage, not a god, not one of Rama's friends. A rakshasa, Rama's old enemy, who was once hurled across the sea by him. That's what gives the words their weight. He has met Rama as an enemy, and he speaks from that. And he's using everything he knows to try to save his own king from himself.
screen: `BECOME A GOLDEN DEER.` · `PLEASANT WORDS ARE EASY TO FIND.` · `RAMA IS DHARMA IN BODILY FORM.` · `THE WARNING FROM AN OLD ENEMY.` · then, large: `TRYING TO SAVE HIS KING.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Bring to mind one person who has told you something you didn't want to hear, that turned out to be true. Picture their face as they said it. Notice what it cost them to say it. Then let a little gratitude toward them rise. If someone comes to mind whom you've been meaning to tell a hard truth, kindly, just hold that too, without planning. Breathe steadily. The bell holds the time.
Dharma, right living, duty, truth: Maricha tells Ravana that flatterers are easy to find, but Rama is dharma in bodily form.
Your line: pleasant things are easy to find. Today, listen all the way through to one thing you'd rather not hear. Day five hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Maricha's line ramo vigrahavan dharmah, Rama is dharma in bodily form, is quoted on its own in Hindu teaching, as are his lines on rare, honest advice.

match.prompt: the second visit — tap the pairs.
pairs: a golden deer with silver spots
one who speaks and hears hard truth

myth: the famous line that Rama is dharma in bodily form is spoken by a sage
it's spoken by Maricha, a rakshasa and Rama's old enemy.
Maricha says Rama wasn't exiled for any crime
he went to keep his father's word.
Ravana flies to Maricha alone on the second visit
in his chariot, along the coast.

fork.setup: you're Maricha. your king wants you to lure Rama away so he can steal Sita. what do you tell him?
options: the hard truth: Rama is dharma itself, and this will ruin you.
fork.reveal: Maricha tells him the hard truth, plainly. tomorrow: what Ravana does with it.

original.note: Sanskrit: 'Rama is dharma with a body,' Maricha's line in Aranya 37.

trapdoor: what you thought: Maricha is just Ravana's helper.
what it means: he's the one who warns Ravana, and calls Rama dharma itself.
what a scholar hears: Aranya 37 holds both the verse on rare honest advice and 'ramo vigrahavan dharmah', two lines that stand on their own as sayings.
recall: rises from the fire to Brahma's world
